feed.title: Equilibrium Daily
feed.subtitle: One short note a day, each stating and proving one result in economics or finance. Notes are drafted by AI and reviewed before publication.

entry.title: One More Trader Always Helps in Nested Symmetric Markets: A Note on Rostek and Weretka (2012)
entry.summary: Rostek and Weretka (2012) show that in small markets a larger market can have a less informative price, because entry can lower commonality, the average correlation between traders' values. Within their symmetric framework, a single trader added to a market without changing the incumbents' correlations cannot lower commonality, so the price becomes more informative with every entrant. Information dilution needs traders to arrive in groups or incumbents' correlations to change.
entry.content:
Rostek and Weretka (2012) show that in small markets a larger market can have a less informative price, because entry can lower commonality, the average correlation between traders' values. Within their symmetric framework, a single trader added to a market without changing the incumbents' correlations cannot lower commonality, so the price becomes more informative with every entrant. Information dilution needs traders to arrive in groups or incumbents' correlations to change.

Result. If an equicommonal correlation matrix is extended by one trader, keeping the incumbents' correlations, and the extended matrix is again equicommonal, the entrant's correlation with every incumbent equals the existing commonality barrho, so commonality is unchanged; along any such sequence barrho >= 0 is constant and price informativeness strictly increases with every entrant when barrho > 0, converging to sigma^2 barrho/(1 + sigma^2 - barrho). Entry in groups can lower informativeness with all correlations preserved: with independent pairs of correlation 1/2 and sigma^2 = 1, moving from two pairs to three lowers it from 1/55 to 1/95.

In the model of Rostek and Weretka (2012), price informativeness depends on market size and on commonality, and at fixed commonality it rises with size, so growth can reduce informativeness only by lowering commonality. Their Section 4.3 explains non-monotone informativeness through a decomposition that assumes each auction results from adding a trader to the previous one with pairwise correlations preserved. Read within the paper's framework, in which every finite auction is equicommonal because the symmetric equilibrium and the informativeness formula are defined only for such auctions, a row-sum argument shows that a single entrant must correlate with each incumbent at exactly the existing commonality, so commonality cannot move and informativeness rises with every entrant. The paper's spatial model, with declining commonality, cannot be generated this way, and its group model grows two traders at a time; group entry can dilute information, as an example with correlated pairs shows. The note also corrects three smaller points: Lemma 1's condition does not make the average value converge, as an example with sectors of doubling size shows, and a Hilbert-space argument gives the exact repair; Proposition 4's entry criterion fails when commonality changes sign, where the correct criterion is that the new commonality lies outside the interval between the two roots; and the constant in Proposition 5 should be the reciprocal of the determinant. The paper's finite-market comparisons, in which the correlation matrix may change freely with size, are unaffected.

Full note with proof (PDF)

entry.title: The Bandit-Auction Index of Pavan, Segal and Toikka, Taken Literally
entry.summary: Pavan, Segal and Toikka (2014) show how to sell to buyers who learn their values by consuming, allocating each period to the buyer with the highest virtual index. Their formula takes the expectation of a ratio of discounted sums, while the index that makes such rules optimal is a ratio of expectations. Taken literally, the printed formula undervalues experimentation and refuses trials that the optimal mechanism makes; the general theorems of the paper are unaffected.
entry.content:
Pavan, Segal and Toikka (2014) show how to sell to buyers who learn their values by consuming, allocating each period to the buyer with the highest virtual index. Their formula takes the expectation of a ratio of discounted sums, while the index that makes such rules optimal is a ratio of expectations. Taken literally, the printed formula undervalues experimentation and refuses trials that the optimal mechanism makes; the general theorems of the paper are unaffected.

Result. The virtual index in equation (15) of Pavan, Segal and Toikka (2014) places the expectation outside a discounted-reward ratio, whereas the Gittins index, a ratio of expectations, is the one that makes an index rule optimal. In a one-buyer example satisfying the paper's assumptions, with delta = 1/2 and initial value v ~ U(0,1), every individually rational, incentive-compatible mechanism implementing the printed rule earns at most 0.63133, while a simple incentive-compatible mechanism earns 0.63335. The index also freezes the current cost, and with costs that vary over time an index rule need not be optimal.

In the bandit auction a seller allocates one unit per period among buyers whose values change only when they are served, and the optimal mechanism awards the unit to the highest virtual index. As printed, the index averages realized discounted rewards along each path and then takes expectations; it coincides with the Gittins index only for fixed stopping dates. In a one-buyer example where the first purchase reveals a standard normal shock, the printed index caps the value of continuing after good news at one half, so buyers with initial values between 0.362 and 0.400 are never served although trying them is profitable. Every incentive-compatible mechanism implementing the printed rule therefore earns at most 0.63133, against 0.63335 for a mechanism that sells one unit and then an option to buy all future units, which is globally incentive compatible and attains the virtual surplus of the Gittins rule. Because the index holds today's cost fixed, a buyer can be served even when every sale has negative virtual surplus under the true time-varying costs, and with such costs the arms are no longer standard bandits. Smaller points: the handicap is described with the wrong sign, the regularity condition should bound absolute moments of the innovations rather than their means, and the nonlinear autoregressive example needs the extra curvature condition of the Supplemental Material, without which two incentive constraints fail. The envelope formula, revenue equivalence and the implementability theorems are untouched.

Full note with proof (PDF)

entry.title: Publish the Rest: Research Funded by Trading Rents in a Kyle-Back Market
entry.summary: Much research is paid for by the trading profits it makes possible, but keeping it private drives liquidity traders away. In a Kyle-Back market with endogenous participation, if all output must stay private the best signal is coarse, and every Gaussian private signal can be worse than no research. If part of the output can be published, the optimum keeps private only a small Gaussian component whose trading rent exactly covers the research bill and publishes the rest.
entry.content:
Much research is paid for by the trading profits it makes possible, but keeping it private drives liquidity traders away. In a Kyle-Back market with endogenous participation, if all output must stay private the best signal is coarse, and every Gaussian private signal can be worse than no research. If part of the output can be published, the optimum keeps private only a small Gaussian component whose trading rent exactly covers the research bill and publishes the rest.

Result. In a Kyle-Back market where liquidity traders with uniformly distributed benefits choose whether to participate, research costing F with information budget k nats can be funded through trading rents if and only if F <= B/4 and d_F <= R_k, where n_F = (1 + sqrt1 - 4F/B)/2, d_F = F^2/(kappa^2 n_F) and R_k = 1 - e^-2k. Over all joint public and private experiments, maximal welfare is B(n_F - n_F^2/2) + eta R_k - F, attained by keeping private only an independent normal component of variance d_F and publishing a normal component of variance R_k - d_F; this split also maximizes price informativeness at every trading date. If all output must stay private, a threshold signal can be optimal over all experiments.

The insider's profit is a loss to liquidity traders, who participate only if their benefits exceed it, so the high participation equilibrium solves kappa a = Bsqrtn(1 - n), where a is the insider's profit coefficient from the Kyle-Back pricing of any signal. Because a lies between the explained variance r and sqrtr, with ordered categories at the bottom and normal signals at the top, a coarse signal can sustain a market that equally accurate normal information would shut down. When all research output must stay private, welfare is bounded by a strictly concave function of participation and a threshold signal attains the bound: with B = kappa = eta = 1, F = 0.1 and a one-bit budget the optimum is the signal 1{V > 1.312}, with welfare 0.633 against 0.5 without research, while every Gaussian private signal does worse than no research. When the producer can publish, the private component only needs to earn the rent that pays for the research, and normal information earns the most rent per unit of private variance, so the global optimum over all joint experiments keeps private a Gaussian component of variance d_F and publishes the rest; in the example the private part explains 0.011 of fundamental variance, the public part 0.739, and welfare rises to 1.144. With research costing F + ck, the optimal amount solves a strictly concave problem in which each unit of cost is scaled up by n/(2n - 1), the liquidity lost to finance one more unit of rent.

Full note with proof (PDF)

entry.title: Noise Beats Coarseness: The Value of Inside Information in the Kyle-Back Model
entry.summary: Two signals that explain the same share of a normal fundamental's variance can be worth very different amounts to an insider in the continuous-time Kyle model. The sign of the fundamental explains 63.7 percent of its variance and earns 63.7 percent of the full-information profit, while normal noisy information of the same precision earns 79.8 percent. The insider must steer order flow to a normally distributed endpoint to stay hidden, so information whose shape is far from normal is worth less.
entry.content:
Two signals that explain the same share of a normal fundamental's variance can be worth very different amounts to an insider in the continuous-time Kyle model. The sign of the fundamental explains 63.7 percent of its variance and earns 63.7 percent of the full-information profit, while normal noisy information of the same precision earns 79.8 percent. The insider must steer order flow to a normally distributed endpoint to stay hidden, so information whose shape is far from normal is worth less.

Result. In the Kyle-Back model with a normal fundamental, for any signal the insider's profit as a share of the full-information profit lies between R^2 and R, where R^2 is the share of fundamental variance the signal explains. The upper bound holds exactly when the insider's valuation is normal, and the lower bound exactly when it is a nondecreasing function of the fundamental, as for information that sorts the fundamental into ordered categories. Among signals with at most n messages the best is the Lloyd-Max quantizer cell of the normal law, earning 1 - D_n: 0.637, 0.810 and 0.883 for n = 2, 3, 4.

In Back's (1992) equilibrium the insider's expected profit equals sigma_u times the largest covariance between his valuation and a standard normal variable, because total order flow must end at a normal point for the insider to stay hidden. Cauchy-Schwarz gives the upper bound R, attained only by normal valuations, and coupling the valuation with the fundamental itself gives the lower bound R^2, attained exactly by monotone coarse information such as the sign of the fundamental, thresholds or interval categories. In general the profit share is Rrho, where rho is the largest correlation between the valuation and a normal variable: 2/pi in square root for two-point laws, 0.977 for uniform and 0.910 for Student t_3. With n messages the best signal reports the Lloyd-Max cell, with thresholds at pm 0.612sigma_v for three categories and at 0 and pm 0.982sigma_v for four, and noise or randomization cannot help; by Shannon's bound one bit of information is worth at most sqrt3/2 of perfect foresight. Two consequences follow inside the model. The covariation of price changes with order flow equals the value of information for every signal; the ratio of fundamental variance to price impact divides it by (Rrho)^2, overstating the value of sign information by (pi/2)^2 = 2.47, and the ratio of price variance to price impact divides it by rho^2, still overstating it by pi/2. Non-normal information also reaches prices more slowly: by date t prices reflect at most the share t of the insider's information, and for sign information the share is (2/pi)arcsin t, one third at t = 1/2.

Full note with proof (PDF)

entry.title: The Feldstein-Horioka Puzzle Is Back
entry.summary: Feldstein and Horioka (1980) found that countries that save more also invest more, almost one for one, as if capital could not cross borders. By the mid-2000s the link had nearly vanished. In World Bank data up to 2024 it has returned: across OECD countries, about half of a country's extra saving again shows up as extra investment at home, as in the 1980s, because current-account imbalances have shrunk.
entry.content:
Feldstein and Horioka (1980) found that countries that save more also invest more, almost one for one, as if capital could not cross borders. By the mid-2000s the link had nearly vanished. In World Bank data up to 2024 it has returned: across OECD countries, about half of a country's extra saving again shows up as extra investment at home, as in the 1980s, because current-account imbalances have shrunk.

Result. Across the 38 OECD countries, the slope of the period-average investment rate on the period-average national saving rate fell from 0.56 in 1980-89 and 0.65 in 1990-99 to 0.16 (s.e. 0.11) in 2000-07 and has returned to 0.51 (s.e. 0.06) in 2016-24; across all countries with population above one million it rose from 0.00 to 0.54 (s.e. 0.06).

If capital moved freely, a country's investment would not depend on its own saving, yet Feldstein and Horioka (1980) found a cross-country slope of investment on saving close to 0.9 for 16 OECD countries in 1960-74. Using the World Development Indicators for 1980-2024, the note runs the same regression for successive periods, one observation per country, with robust standard errors. Because the current account equals saving minus investment, the slope equals 1 - cov(CA,S)/var(S) and falls when high savers run large surpluses. The OECD slope fell to 0.16 in 2000-07 and is 0.51 in 2016-24, with 2008-15 in between at 0.43; the rebound survives a balanced panel, dropping financial centers and oil exporters, using domestic instead of national saving, and counting only fixed investment, and in the euro area excluding Ireland and Luxembourg the slope moved from about zero to 0.41. The mechanism is in the current accounts: their cross-country standard deviation rose from 2.5% of GDP in the 1980s to 5.9% in 2000-07 and is now 3.9%, while the spread of saving rates changed little. The slope summarizes how far investment tracks saving and is not a clean measure of capital mobility, but it implies that about half of a gap in national saving now shows up as a gap in domestic investment.

Full note with proof (PDF)

entry.title: Rough Heston Variance at Zero: Negative Moments, Conditional Paths and a Test for the Zero Event
entry.summary: In the rough Heston model the instantaneous variance is exactly zero with positive probability at every date. Without drift, the variance also puts so much probability just above zero that the expected inverse variance is infinite even after the zero atom is excluded. One root of a Gamma-function equation sets both how much probability lies near zero and how fast the expected variance falls into a zero.
entry.content:
In the rough Heston model the instantaneous variance is exactly zero with positive probability at every date. Without drift, the variance also puts so much probability just above zero that the expected inverse variance is infinite even after the zero atom is excluded. One root of a Gamma-function equation sets both how much probability lies near zero and how fast the expected variance falls into a zero.

Result. In the drift-free rough Heston model with Hurst parameter H in (0, 1/2), E[V_t^-q; V_t > 0] < infinity if and only if q < delta_beta, where delta_beta = (p_beta - beta)/(2H) in (0,1) and p_beta solves a Gamma-function equation, so E[V_t^-1; V_t > 0] = infinity for every H. Conditional on V_T = 0, the expected variance path is v sum_n A_n (1 - s/T)^rho_n with positive weights summing to one and leading exponent rho_beta = 2H(1 + delta_beta), and {V_T = 0} = {integral_0^T V_s (T-s)^-2H-1 ds < infinity} almost surely.

The rough Heston variance reaches zero with positive probability at every fixed date, and without drift the atom is known in closed form. Using the affine transform formula and the maximal solution of the fractional Riccati equation, the note compares the gap between the maximal and unit Riccati solutions with powers of time through a first-contact property of the Riemann-Liouville derivative. This shows that negative moments on the event of positive variance are finite exactly below a cutoff delta_beta, which lies strictly between zero and one for every Hurst parameter (about 0.26 at H = 0.25, 0.59 at H = 0.1 and 0.08 at H = 0.4), and that log P(0 < V_t <= x)/log x -> delta_beta. Conditioning on zero variance at T adds an explicit drift, and the conditional mean solves a renewal equation whose Laplace transform is 1/Psi with Psi(z) = z + lambda_beta Gamma(z+1)/Gamma(z+beta); it is a positive mixture of powers of the time remaining, led by rho_beta = 2H(1 + delta_beta) with second exponent exactly 2beta. The zero event coincides with finiteness of one weighted integral of past variance, whose conditional mean is proportional to minus the log probability of the zero, an instance of the entropy-energy identity. Finally, two exact solutions driven by the same Brownian motion can separate only by changing sign from the first instant; pathwise uniqueness remains open.

Full note with proof (PDF)

entry.title: No-Arbitrage Does Not Imply an Equivalent Calibrated Pricing Measure
entry.summary: When a stock trades over two dates and options on its final price are priced by the market, one usually expects that ruling out arbitrage guarantees a pricing measure that agrees with the physical probabilities on which events are possible, prices every option correctly and makes the stock a fair game. In a simple, well-behaved market this fails: there is no arbitrage, yet every pricing measure that fits the option prices ignores a state that has physical probability one half.
entry.content:
When a stock trades over two dates and options on its final price are priced by the market, one usually expects that ruling out arbitrage guarantees a pricing measure that agrees with the physical probabilities on which events are possible, prices every option correctly and makes the stock a fair game. In a simple, well-behaved market this fails: there is no arbitrage, yet every pricing measure that fits the option prices ignores a state that has physical probability one half.

Result. In a two-date semistatic market with bounded prices, a physical law P that is itself a martingale, and option-implied terminal law nu with 1/2 <= dP_Y/dnu < 3/2, there is no arbitrage, yet no calibrated martingale measure is equivalent to P: the only calibrated martingale measure absolutely continuous with respect to P gives zero probability to an intermediate state of physical probability 1/2. In the family of such chain markets with weights (t_n), no-arbitrage holds if and only if sum_n 2^n t_n = infinity, while an equivalent calibrated martingale measure exists if and only if inf_k 2^2k t_2k > 0.

Nutz, Wiesel and Zhao (2023) assume a calibrated martingale measure equivalent to the physical law with finite relative entropy and leave its characterization in terms of trading strategies as an open problem. The note shows that ordinary no-arbitrage is not that characterization. The counterexample links infinitely many two-point martingale rows in a single chain with weights t_n = 2^-n/(n log 2), plus one extra row of physical probability one half. Calibrating to the terminal law propagates any weight on the extra row along the chain with alternating sign, so some even row would need negative probability; an arbitrage exploiting this would need an option payoff that doubles at each step down the chain, which is not integrable. The construction extends the non-closedness of semistatic outcomes found by Acciaio, Larsson and Schachermayer (2017) to a regular setting with a fixed physical law. With a closure condition the characterization returns through known results: by the Kreps-Yan theorem an equivalent calibrated measure exists if and only if the weak-star closure of the superhedging cone contains no free lunch, and a finite-entropy one exists if and only if no sequence of trades drives the expected exponential shortfall of a loss on any event down to its no-loss value.

Full note with proof (PDF)

entry.title: Urban Growth Replicates, With Three Fixes
entry.summary: Duranton and Puga (2023) estimate that relaxing planning limits in seven expensive US cities would raise national output by about 8%. An independent rewrite of their public code reproduces every headline number exactly, and that figure survives. Three coding errors change smaller numbers: freezing cities at their 1950 sizes costs about a fifth of consumption rather than a quarter, and Los Angeles enters the policy by only 22 dollars.
entry.content:
Duranton and Puga (2023) estimate that relaxing planning limits in seven expensive US cities would raise national output by about 8%. An independent rewrite of their public code reproduces every headline number exactly, and that figure survives. Three coding errors change smaller numbers: freezing cities at their 1950 sizes costs about a fifth of consumption rather than a quarter, and Los Angeles enters the policy by only 22 dollars.

Result. Re-coded from the authors' public files, the headline results of Duranton and Puga (2023) reproduce to six decimals, including the 7.95% output gain when seven cities expand. Three coding errors are confirmed: the consumption loss from freezing cities at their 1950 sizes is 19.4%, not 26.8%; the seven-city consumption gain is 2.11%, not 2.16%; and Los Angeles clears the policy's 200,000 dollar price cutoff by 22 dollars under a conversion that depends on the omitted city, although every standard conversion keeps it in. City edges spread with population at elasticity 0.41 rather than the model's 1, but urban costs measured directly rise at elasticity 0.104, close to the model's 0.11.

Duranton and Puga (2023) model incumbents who use planning rules to cap city size and find that relaxing permits in seven expensive US cities would raise output by 7.95%. Porting the authors' Stata programs to Python reproduces their regressions and every headline number; only regressions on restricted NLSY79 and NHTS locations could not be re-run. Three errors are confirmed. Log prices are converted to dollars with the squared standard error of each city dummy, which depends on the omitted city: Los Angeles clears the cutoff by 22 dollars, misses it by 302 dollars (output gain 5.68%) with itself omitted or with no correction, and lies between 226,000 and 229,000 dollars under residual variance, Duan smearing or full prediction variance, which keep the same seven cities. The frozen-city calculation credits newcomers with incumbent consumption, contrary to the paper's own accounting, so the loss is 19.4% rather than 26.8%; the original figure holds only if permit payments are rebated, in which case the seven-city consumption gain would be 4.15%. Stata's min() ignoring missing values drops 774,360 residents of ten emptied cities, and counting them moves that gain from 2.16% to 2.11%. Equation (29)'s exact Pareto distribution of city sizes requires continuous time, although approximate Zipf survives. The linear city implies edge distance proportional to population, while the data give elasticity 0.41 (s.e. 0.02); center house prices plus marginal consumption rise at 0.104 (s.e. 0.010), close to the model's cost elasticity of 0.11, so the mechanism holds in reduced form.

Full note with proof (PDF)

entry.title: Five Small Errors in Bayesian Persuasion
entry.summary: Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) founded information design, and a line-by-line check confirms its main theorems: with finitely many states, the sender's best signal is found by concavifying his payoff, an optimum exists, and it needs no more signal realizations than there are states. Five statements in the fine print are wrong as written, including a popular rule of thumb that two concave functions mean persuasion cannot help, and the web appendix's formula for infinitely many states. Each has a one-line fix.
entry.content:
Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) founded information design, and a line-by-line check confirms its main theorems: with finitely many states, the sender's best signal is found by concavifying his payoff, an optimum exists, and it needs no more signal realizations than there are states. Five statements in the fine print are wrong as written, including a popular rule of thumb that two concave functions mean persuasion cannot help, and the web appendix's formula for infinitely many states. Each has a one-line fix.

Result. The main theorems of Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) hold, but five statements do not: (1) with infinitely many states the value must be the closed convex hull, the smallest upper semicontinuous concave function above hat v, since in an example meeting all the web appendix's assumptions its formula gives the sender 0 while full revelation gives 1; (2) a concave receiver action and a concave sender payoff do not rule out gains from persuasion, as with action sqrtp and sender payoff -a; (3) in the lobbying application with alpha < 1/2, no disclosure is optimal but not uniquely; (4) a worked example ignores the constraint a >= 0, so its bound is (1 + E[omega])/2 rather than 1; (5) Proposition 2's genericity claim needs every action to be uniquely optimal at some belief.

Bayesian persuasion characterizes the sender's optimal value as the concave closure of his payoff as a function of the receiver's belief; with finitely many states this is correct, an optimum exists and at most as many signal realizations as states are needed, and an exact-arithmetic check on 200 random finite games agrees. The web appendix's extension to compact state spaces uses the convex hull without closure, which contains only finite mixtures of beliefs: with a state uniform on [0,1] and a receiver who guesses only when certain, every finite signal yields 0 for the sender while full revelation yields 1, and the fix is the closed convex hull, under which existence survives. The rule of thumb that persuasion cannot help when the receiver's action and the sender's payoff are both concave fails because composing concave functions preserves concavity only if the outer function is increasing: with action sqrtp and sender payoff -a, full disclosure beats silence at p = 1/4 (-1/4 against -1/2). In the lobbying application any signal that keeps every posterior mean at the prior mean is optimal for alpha < 1/2, a worked example's bound becomes 1/2 against a true optimum of 1/3 once negative actions are ruled out, and Proposition 2 needs the stronger assumption that every action is uniquely optimal at some belief, which the web appendix already states. None of the errors affects the main theorems, but the rule of thumb is the kind of shortcut applied work reuses, and the appendix formula is cited as the reference result for continuous states.

Full note with proof (PDF)

entry.title: Does Stamp Duty Make UK Shares Cheap? Prices Say No, Takeovers Say Maybe
entry.summary: The UK charges a 0.5% tax every time a UK share is bought, and a common argument holds that this makes UK shares cheap and UK companies easy takeover targets. If buyers priced in every future payment of the tax, the discount would be about 3% for the median stock and larger for stocks that trade often. In the two settings where only the tax differs, prices show no such discount; the only support comes from takeover bids, and it may reflect UK takeover rules rather than the tax.
entry.content:
The UK charges a 0.5% tax every time a UK share is bought, and a common argument holds that this makes UK shares cheap and UK companies easy takeover targets. If buyers priced in every future payment of the tax, the discount would be about 3% for the median stock and larger for stocks that trade often. In the two settings where only the tax differs, prices show no such discount; the only support comes from takeover bids, and it may reflect UK takeover rules rather than the tax.

Result. If buyers capitalize all future stamp duty, a UK share's price discount is about 0.005 T/r, where T is annual turnover and r the discount rate. When the tax on AIM shares was abolished (announced 20 March 2013), the slope of AIM returns on turnover was -0.0025 (s.e. 0.0012) against a predicted +0.0625, and the taxed London line of Unilever traded on average 0.2% above its untaxed Dutch twin in 2006-2020 against a predicted 3.4% below. Across 15 European markets, UK bid probability rises with turnover more steeply than in untaxed markets, but a within-UK test cannot rule out no effect.

The UK's 0.5% stamp duty on share purchases is often blamed for cheap UK valuations, foreign investors' retreat and takeovers of UK companies; if buyers capitalize every future payment, the price discount is about 0.005 T/r, around 3% for the median UK stock with r = 8\%. When AIM shares became exempt in 2013-14, AIM stocks beat still-taxed small Main Market firms by only 0.49% on the announcement day, an unremarkable spread, and frequently traded stocks gained no more than rarely traded ones, although the tax predicts up to a 5.5% gain; AIM turnover rose by about 3.5%, but foreign institutional ownership did not change measurably. Companies with two share lines show no tax discount either: Unilever's London line traded at parity with its Dutch twin for 14 years, Carnival's London line traded at a premium for most of 2004-16, and RELX's London line traded 3.8% above its Dutch line in 2015-18. Across 109,000 firm-years in 15 European markets, UK companies whose shares trade more are more likely to receive a bid, more steeply than in untaxed markets, but this cross-country pattern may reflect UK takeover rules, and the within-UK test after the AIM exemption is too imprecise to confirm it. The estimates are presented as first-pass and differ from earlier evidence that UK prices rose when stamp duty was cut from 2% in the 1980s.

Full note with proof (PDF)

entry.title: Do US Firm Sizes Follow Zipf's Law? In the Middle, Yes. At the Top, No
entry.summary: Axtell (2001) found that US firm sizes follow Zipf's law: a firm ten times larger is ten times rarer, from the smallest firms to the largest. In public data up to 2023 this holds remarkably well between about 5 and 10,000 employees, but not at the top: Zipf predicts a largest US firm of about 12 million employees, while the largest actual employer has about 2 million worldwide. The giants are too few and too small, which matters because Zipf is the case in which shocks to the largest firms move the whole economy.
entry.content:
Axtell (2001) found that US firm sizes follow Zipf's law: a firm ten times larger is ten times rarer, from the smallest firms to the largest. In public data up to 2023 this holds remarkably well between about 5 and 10,000 employees, but not at the top: Zipf predicts a largest US firm of about 12 million employees, while the largest actual employer has about 2 million worldwide. The giants are too few and too small, which matters because Zipf is the case in which shocks to the largest firms move the whole economy.

Result. In the Census Business Dynamics Statistics for 1978-2023, the share of US firms with at least s employees falls like s^-alpha with alpha between 0.94 and 1.00 for 5 <= s <= 10,000 in every year, as Zipf's law requires. The law fails at the top: the mean size of firms with 10,000 or more employees implies a tail exponent of about 1.32 in 2023 (a Hill estimate of 1.29 on the 200 largest Compustat employers), and on employees, sales and market value alike the 50 largest listed firms have exponents between about 1.4 and 1.9.

Zipf's law for firm sizes, Pr(S >= s) propto s^-alpha with alpha = 1, is the benchmark outcome of random proportional growth and governs whether idiosyncratic shocks to large firms matter for aggregate fluctuations (Gabaix 2011). Using the public Census Business Dynamics Statistics for 1978-2023 and Compustat for the largest employers, the note finds slopes between 0.94 and 1.00 from 5 to 10,000 employees in every year, too few firms with 1-4 employees, and a clearly thinner top. Extrapolating Zipf from the 1,210 firms with 10,000 or more employees in 2023 predicts a largest firm of about 12 million employees, against 2.1 million for the largest actual employer, and matching the observed mean of that class requires an exponent of 1.32. By headcount the top has moved toward Zipf, from exponents of 1.7-1.9 in the 1980s and 1990s to about 1.35 today, while the middle of the distribution did not change. Measuring size by sales or market value does not rescue the law: the 500 largest listed firms look Zipf on every measure, but the 50 largest are too similar in size on all of them.

Full note with proof (PDF)

entry.title: Growth in Endogenous Production Networks Needs Compatible Recipes: A Correction to Acemoglu and Azar (2020)
entry.summary: Acemoglu and Azar (2020) show that when firms choose their suppliers, the growth rate equals the rate at which the best technologies improve, multiplied by the full input-output network. That product assumes firms can use the best technology and keep all their important suppliers at the same time. When the best new technologies require dropping an important supplier, firms must give up either productivity or network amplification, and growth falls short of the formula.
entry.content:
Acemoglu and Azar (2020) show that when firms choose their suppliers, the growth rate equals the rate at which the best technologies improve, multiplied by the full input-output network. That product assumes firms can use the best technology and keep all their important suppliers at the same time. When the best new technologies require dropping an important supplier, firms must give up either productivity or network amplification, and growth falls short of the formula.

Result. Under the stated assumptions of Acemoglu and Azar (2020), the growth formula of their Theorem 6, g = D sum_i,j beta_i L_ij with L = (I-alpha)^-1, is false: in an economy that satisfies every assumption and where the formula predicts g = 2, equilibrium growth is 4/3, and a second example gives 4. The formula holds, and the condition is also necessary, under compatibility: for every industry i and every finite set H of suppliers with positive shares, the best recipe that keeps H satisfies M_i^H(t)/t -> D, together with a uniform bound on frontier productivity across industries.

In the endogenous production network model of Acemoglu and Azar (2020), industries choose supplier sets from all available input combinations, and Theorem 6 states that growth equals the frontier productivity rate D times the Leontief multiplier of the full potential network. The note gives two economies that satisfy every stated assumption but contradict the formula. In the first, recipes that use the supplier carrying half of all input shares are unproductive, so every firm drops it and growth is 4/3 rather than 2; the same holds with independent continuous productivity draws, where growth can take any value in [4/3, 2). In the second, late-arriving industries with very high productivity levels raise growth to 4, because the assumption on the frontier holds industry by industry but not uniformly. The failures trace to two specific steps in the proof and overturn Corollaries 1 to 3, the upper bound of Theorem 7 and Theorem B3, while sustained positive growth, the benchmark with iid Gumbel or exponential draws and the static model survive; the corrected theorem holds exactly when frontier technologies are compatible with the existing supplier base.

entry.title: Wisdom of Crowds with Many Separate Groups: A Correction to Golub and Jackson (2010)
entry.summary: Golub and Jackson (2010) showed that a society that averages its neighbors' opinions learns the truth exactly when no one keeps a large influence. That equivalence breaks when the society splits into many separate groups: each group may learn well, yet with so many groups at least one of them is almost sure to end far from the truth. The note gives a counterexample, a corrected statement, and a sharp rule for equal-sized groups: their size must grow faster than the logarithm of their number.
entry.content:
Golub and Jackson (2010) showed that a society that averages its neighbors' opinions learns the truth exactly when no one keeps a large influence. That equivalence breaks when the society splits into many separate groups: each group may learn well, yet with so many groups at least one of them is almost sure to end far from the truth. The note gives a counterexample, a corrected statement, and a sharp rule for equal-sized groups: their size must grow faster than the logarithm of their number.

Result. For networks with a growing number of separate closed groups, vanishing maximal influence s_1(n) -> 0 does not imply wisdom: a society of 4^m groups of m agents satisfies every assumption of Golub and Jackson (2010) with s_1(n) = 1/m, yet with probability 1-(1-2^-m)^4^m -> 1 some agent ends at belief one when the truth is one half. In general, the society is wise if and only if sum_c=1^K_n Pr(|Y_c - mu| > varepsilon) -> 0 for every varepsilon > 0, where Y_c is the consensus of closed group c; the original equivalence holds when the number of groups K_n is bounded, and for K_n equally weighted groups of size m_n with fair-coin signals, the society is wise if and only if m_n -> infinity and (log K_n)/m_n -> 0.

Under naive DeGroot learning, Proposition 2 of Golub and Jackson (2010) states that a sequence of convergent networks is wise, meaning all agents are simultaneously close to the truth, if and only if the largest influence vanishes, and the paper states that its results apply to all convergent networks. The proof shows that each agent learns individually, but wisdom requires all agents to be right at the same time, and with many independent closed groups the two requirements differ: in a network of 4^m groups of m agents with fair-coin signals, the largest influence is 1/m and Theorem 4's balance and minimal in-dispersion conditions hold, yet the probability that some group is unanimously wrong tends to one. The corrected proposition characterizes wisdom by the sum over groups of each group's probability of error, keeps the 'only if' direction, restores the original equivalence when the number of closed groups is bounded (including every strongly connected network), and gives a distribution-free sufficient condition, max_c Q_c (1 + log K_n) -> 0. For equally weighted groups this condition is sharp: using Hoeffding's inequality and a method-of-types bound, the society is wise exactly when group size grows faster than the logarithm of the number of groups. Vanishing maximal influence still makes the society accurate on average, Theorem 1 is not exposed because its out-dispersion condition bounds the number of closed groups, and the paper's central message, that a society learns well only if no agent's influence stays large, is unaffected.

entry.title: Engel's Law Holds for Groceries, Not for Restaurants
entry.summary: Poorer households spend a larger share of their budget on food, and this still holds in US data up to 2024. The pattern comes entirely from groceries: spending on restaurants rises in proportion to the budget in every income group.
entry.content:
Poorer households spend a larger share of their budget on food, and this still holds in US data up to 2024. The pattern comes entirely from groceries: spending on restaurants rises in proportion to the budget in every income group.

Result. In the US Consumer Expenditure Survey, Engel's law holds in every year from 1984 to 2024: across the five income groups the elasticity of food spending with respect to total spending averages 0.77 and is below one in all 41 years. The law is driven entirely by groceries (elasticity 0.58), while spending on food away from home has an elasticity of 1.07, above one in 40 of 41 years.

Engel (1857) observed that poorer families spend a larger share of their budget on food, so that food has an income elasticity below one. Using published BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey means for each income fifth, 1984-2024, the note estimates each year's elasticity as the slope of log spending on log total expenditures across the five groups, separately for all food, groceries and eating out. In 2024 groceries fell from 11.0% of spending in the lowest fifth to 6.2% in the highest, while eating out took between 4.7% and 5.2% in every group; for the average household the food share fell from 14.7% in 1984-1993 to 12.8% in 2005-2019 and has not fallen since. The official US poverty line still rests on Orshansky's multiplier of three times a minimal food budget, whereas 2024 food shares of 15.7% in the lowest fifth and 12.9% on average would imply a multiplier of about 6 to 8. Because eating out rises at least in proportion to the budget, methods that use Engel curves to estimate CPI bias should rely on groceries rather than on all food.

entry.title: The Pythagorean Expectation, 45 Seasons Later
entry.summary: Bill James's formula linking a baseball team's wins to its runs scored and allowed has worked unchanged in the 45 seasons since it was published. Records that beat the formula are mostly luck and do not carry over, so a team's quality is better read from its runs than from its wins.
entry.content:
Bill James's formula linking a baseball team's wins to its runs scored and allowed has worked unchanged in the 45 seasons since it was published. Records that beat the formula are mostly luck and do not carry over, so a team's quality is better read from its runs than from its wins.

Result. Bill James's Pythagorean expectation W/L = (RS/RA)^k survives a 45-season out-of-sample test: the exponent is k = 1.847 on 1901-1980 and k = 1.848 on 1981-2025, the 1901-1980 fit predicts later wins with an error of about 4 per 162 games and explains 88% of their variation, and wins above or below the formula do not persist: about 92% disappears the next season.

The Pythagorean expectation, published around 1980, relates a baseball team's ratio of wins to losses to its ratio of runs scored to runs allowed, and every season after 1980 provides a clean holdout sample. Using 2,706 Major League team-seasons from the Lahman Baseball Database, the note estimates k as the slope of log(W/L) on log(RS/RA) before and after publication and finds the same value to the third decimal, with out-of-sample root mean squared error of 4.06 wins against 4.16 for James's original k = 2. The exponent varies by decade between 1.74 and 1.98 but has no trend, and letting it rise with runs per game does not improve the out-of-sample error. Wins above the formula (luck, with a standard deviation of 4.2 wins) have a next-season correlation of only 0.04 before 1980 and 0.08 after, and in forecasting next season's record the predicted share receives about three times the weight of the actual share. The same task, separating a persistent component from a large transitory one, arises when judging fund managers, executives or forecasters from short records.

entry.title: Who Bargains Next? Recognition and Cooperative Allocations
entry.summary: Who proposes after an offer is rejected looks like a procedural detail, but it changes the outcome of coalitional bargaining. If the player who rejects proposes next, patient players no longer reach the Shapley value: every player's deviation from an equal share is amplified.
entry.content:
Who proposes after an offer is rejected looks like a procedural detail, but it changes the outcome of coalitional bargaining. If the player who rejects proposes next, patient players no longer reach the Shapley value: every player's deviation from an equal share is amplified.

Result. In three-player coalitional bargaining with proposer departure probability q, both protocols have a unique subgame-perfect equilibrium payoff vector with immediate efficient agreement: E_0 = e + d(s-e) when the next proposer after a surviving rejection is drawn uniformly, and E_1 = e + d(1+a)(s-e) when the rejector proposes next, where s is the Shapley value, e the equal split, a = delta(1-q) and d = delta q/(1-a). The patient limits are s and s + (1-q)(s-e), which coincide if and only if c_1 = c_2 = c_3.

Hart and Mas-Colell (1996) showed that random proposers with a risk that a rejected proposer drops out lead patient players to the Shapley value. This note compares two anonymous protocols for three players with transferable utility that share coalition opportunities, discounting and departure risk, and differ only in who proposes after a surviving rejection: a uniformly drawn player (P_0) or the rejector (P_1). Every subgame-perfect equilibrium, including mixed and history-dependent ones, agrees immediately on the grand coalition, and each protocol has a unique payoff vector. Under P_1 every player's patient deviation from the equal share is multiplied by 2-q, so players whose Shapley value exceeds one third gain and the others lose; for q = 7/8 and (c_1, c_2, c_3) = (1/4, 1/20, 1/20) the patient payoffs are (4/15, 11/30, 11/30) under P_0 and (31/120, 89/240, 89/240) under P_1. Specifying who controls bargaining after disagreement is therefore part of specifying the outcome.

entry.title: Zipf's Law for US Cities, 2000-2024
entry.summary: Zipf's law, under which a city's size is inversely proportional to its rank, is often treated as a constant of urban economics. In US data for 2000-2024 it holds only for metropolitan areas at particular cut-offs; incorporated cities follow a clean power law, but with an exponent clearly above 1.
entry.content:
Zipf's law, under which a city's size is inversely proportional to its rank, is often treated as a constant of urban economics. In US data for 2000-2024 it holds only for metropolitan areas at particular cut-offs; incorporated cities follow a clean power law, but with an exponent clearly above 1.

Result. In US data for 2000-2024, Zipf's law with zeta = 1 fails for both common city definitions: for metropolitan areas the exponent for the largest 135 is about 1.1 and not statistically different from 1, but the rank-size relation is curved, so a single power law is rejected; for incorporated cities the relation is straight, but zeta ~ 1.45 is statistically above 1.

Zipf's law says that the number of cities larger than S is proportional to S^-zeta with zeta = 1, the value implied by city growth unrelated to size (Gabaix 1999). Using Census Bureau population files for metropolitan statistical areas (2010, 2020, 2024) and incorporated places (2000, 2010, 2020, 2024), the note estimates zeta by the rank minus one half regression of Gabaix and Ibragimov (2011) and applies their curvature test. For metropolitan areas the curvature statistic is -2.3 to -2.7 for the largest 135 and -3.0 for the largest 250, and the estimate falls from 1.42 for the top 50 to 0.90 for all metros, so zeta is within 0.05 of 1 only for cut-offs between about 190 and 320. For cities proper the curvature statistic is near zero, while zeta is 1.41 to 1.46 for the largest 135 (t of 2.4 to 2.6 against 1). Both patterns are stable from 2000 to 2024, so an exponent of 1 appears only for metropolitan areas at particular cut-offs.

entry.title: The Pre-FOMC Drift Lost Its Morning
entry.summary: Stocks have earned a well-known excess return in the hours before Federal Reserve announcements. Studies using daily closing prices conclude that this drift has faded, but it has moved rather than disappeared: since 2011 it is earned overnight before the announcement day, not during the morning of that day.
entry.content:
Stocks have earned a well-known excess return in the hours before Federal Reserve announcements. Studies using daily closing prices conclude that this drift has faded, but it has moved rather than disappeared: since 2011 it is earned overnight before the announcement day, not during the morning of that day.

Result. The pre-FOMC announcement drift in SPY has not disappeared; its timing has changed. From September 2003 to March 2011 most of it accrued between the open and 2pm on the announcement day (29.1 bp, t = 4.3); after March 2011 that morning component is zero (1.5 bp), and the overnight return into the announcement day (17.2 bp, t = 3.7) is now essentially the whole drift.

Lucca and Moench (2015) documented a large excess stock return in the 24 hours before scheduled FOMC announcements, and studies using daily closing prices report that it weakened after 2015. Using SPY from September 2003 to December 2024 (170 scheduled announcements), with CRSP open and close prices and TAQ quote mid-points at 2pm, the note splits the window from 2pm on the previous day to the close of the following day into seven legs and compares each leg on announcement days with all other days. The 2pm-to-2pm drift falls from 58.0 bp to 16.9 bp, and the fall of 27.6 bp in the morning leg has t = -3.6, while the overnight leg is stable at about 13 to 17 bp and holds separately in 2011-2015 and 2016-2024. Closing-price studies understate the remaining drift because returns after the announcement have been weak since 2011. The overnight result survives alternative price sources, the exclusion of 2020, winsorization, placebo nights and the removal of the 2011-2012 meetings with a 12:30pm statement.

entry.title: The Information Complexity of Nash Equilibrium
entry.summary: How many noisy observations of payoffs are needed to find an approximate Nash equilibrium of a small zero-sum game with high confidence? The answer depends only on the equilibrium mixing probabilities, is largest when equilibrium play is uniform, and can be far smaller than estimating every payoff first and then solving the game.
entry.content:
How many noisy observations of payoffs are needed to find an approximate Nash equilibrium of a small zero-sum game with high confidence? The answer depends only on the equilibrium mixing probabilities, is largest when equilibrium play is uniform, and can be far smaller than estimating every payoff first and then solving the game.

Result. For a 3 x 3 zero-sum game A with a unique, completely mixed equilibrium (p,q), learned from noisy N(A_ij,1) queries, the expected number of observations needed to return an varepsilon-equilibrium with probability 1-delta satisfies lim_varepsilon decreasing to 0 varepsilon^2 lim_delta decreasing to 0 fracM_varepsilon,delta(A)log(1/delta) = C(p,q) := 2[min_w in Delta_9^circ F_p,q(w)]^2, with 0 < C(p,q) <= 8 and C(p,q) = 8 if and only if p = q = (1/3,1/3,1/3).

Each query of payoff entry (i,j) returns an independent N(A_ij,1) observation, and a procedure must return strategies with duality gap at most varepsilon with probability at least 1-delta for every game in the class. The leading observation complexity, as confidence and then accuracy increase, is the constant C(p,q), which depends on the game only through its equilibrium probabilities; F_p,q(w) is a transport-type functional over couplings of p and q given a sampling allocation w over the nine entries. The constant is maximal, equal to 8, exactly at uniform equilibrium, and for the family A_r with equilibrium (1-2r, r, r) it is of order r^2. By comparison, estimating all nine payoffs to maximum-norm error varepsilon has coefficient 18, and estimating payoffs to error varepsilon/2 and then solving the game has coefficient 72. The proof applies the infinite-answer pure-exploration characterization of Poiani, Bernasconi and Celli (2026) and evaluates its small-accuracy limit through transportation duality.

entry.title: The Price of a Place in Line
entry.summary: A regulator must decide whose infrastructure project goes first but cannot verify how valuable or reliable a developer's project is. Collateral is then the only tool that makes developers report truthfully. The note computes the exact deposit needed for efficient priority, shows that it exceeds what either pivotal developer gains from priority, and shows that a priority lottery is optimal when collateral is scarcer.
entry.content:
A regulator must decide whose infrastructure project goes first but cannot verify how valuable or reliable a developer's project is. Collateral is then the only tool that makes developers report truthfully. The note computes the exact deposit needed for efficient priority, shows that it exceeds what either pivotal developer gains from priority, and shows that a priority lottery is optimal when collateral is scarcer.

Result. Efficient truthful implementation with individual rationality is possible if and only if the escrow limit satisfies L >= K, where K = (c[s(1-r)a - r(1-s)b])/(s-r); moreover K > csa, so the required collateral exceeds both pivotal types' expected gains from priority.

A developer whose project value v in {a,b} and completion probability p in {r,s} are private competes for priority against a fallback developer with a publicly known type; the second project is attempted only if the first fails, and project values are unverifiable. The regulator can use only an escrow of at most L, refunded according to reports, the priority lottery and observed completion outcomes. Efficiency gives priority exactly to high-value reports, although the pivotal high-value type h=(b,r) values priority less than the low-value type ell=(a,s). When L < K, every DSIC mechanism has expected welfare loss at least min{mu_hDelta_h, mu_ell(-Delta_ell)}(1-L/K)_+, and a priority lottery attains this bound for a family of two-point priors. The implementing deposit refunds more after failure than after success.
